analysis.one_liner: Pauses US arms sales to Saudi security agencies until the President certifies it stops hunting dissidents.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 350-71 on April 21, 2021, but it sat in the Senate Foreign Relations Committee without a vote until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill stops US arms sales and exports to Saudi intelligence, internal security, and law enforcement agencies for 120 days, and keeps them stopped unless the President periodically certifies that Saudi Arabia is not killing or intimidating dissidents abroad, unjustly imprisoning US citizens and green-card holders, or torturing detainees. It also requires the President to certify that Saudi diplomats are not using their credentials to track or harass Saudi nationals living in the United States, closing at least one Saudi diplomatic facility if they are. It directs reports on Saudi harassment of people in the US and on whether US intelligence fulfilled its duty to warn Jamal Khashoggi, a US-resident Saudi journalist killed in the Saudi consulate in Istanbul in 2018, of threats to his life.
analysis.who_benefits: Saudi dissidents, journalists, and critics living in the United States; US citizens and green-card holders who could be detained or blocked from leaving Saudi Arabia; and anyone at risk of being tracked or harassed by Saudi agents using diplomatic credentials in this country.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Saudi dissidents and critics living in the US

how_it_helps.text: Bars new US defense sales, export licenses, and transfers to Saudi intelligence, internal security, and law enforcement agencies for 120 days.

Keeps those restrictions in place for up to three years unless the President certifies, every 120 days, that Saudi Arabia has not forcibly repatriated, intimidated, or killed dissidents abroad, unjustly imprisoned US citizens or lawful permanent residents, or tortured detainees.

Requires the President to certify that Saudi diplomatic personnel are not using diplomatic credentials or facilities to surveil or harass Saudi nationals in the US; if the President cannot, he must close one or more Saudi diplomatic or consular facilities until he can.

Orders reports on whether Saudi officials have systematically harassed or intimidated people in the United States and whether US intelligence agencies fulfilled their duty to warn Khashoggi of the threats to his life.

analysis.who_pays: Defense contractors would lose a sales channel to Saudi security agencies while the restrictions last, and the President would lose discretion to keep arms flowing without certifying Saudi behavior. Sales for the external defense of Saudi territory are exempt, so the bulk of the broader US-Saudi arms trade would continue.
analysis.who_pays_short: Defense contractors selling to Saudi security agencies

drawbacks.text: The President can waive the restrictions by declaring, 15 days in advance, that a waiver is in the vital national security interests of the United States, giving the executive an escape hatch.

The certification standard turns on the US government's own determinations: sales resume unless the government itself has found abuses, so a willing administration could keep certifying without consequences for Saudi Arabia.

The ban covers only sales to intelligence, internal security, and law enforcement agencies; arms sold for the defense of Saudi territory from external threats are explicitly exempt, leaving most of the weapons trade untouched.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the people it protects, the bill is a real safeguard: it ties arms sales to Saudi conduct toward dissidents and to the safety of people in the US, and it forces public reporting on both. Its limits are significant: the external-defense exemption leaves the core of the US-Saudi arms trade intact, and the self-certification structure plus a national-security waiver mean an administration that wanted to keep selling could do so. The cost falls narrowly on defense exporters and the executive's discretion, not on ordinary Americans.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 350-71, but it was referred to the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, which never brought it to a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Gerald Connolly introduced the bill on February 26, 2021, following the release of a US intelligence assessment finding that Saudi Arabia's Crown Prince approved the operation to capture or kill Jamal Khashoggi.
The House Foreign Affairs Committee marked up the bill on March 25, 2021, and ordered it reported as amended by voice vote.
The House passed the bill under a suspension-of-the-rules procedure, which requires a two-thirds majority, by a vote of 350-71 on April 21, 2021.
Every House Democrat present voted yes (214-0), and 136 House Republicans voted yes while 71 voted no.
The Senate received the bill on April 22, 2021, and referred it to the Committee on Foreign Relations; it never received a Senate vote before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without a Senate vote, defense contractors kept their unrestricted sales channels to Saudi security agencies, and the Saudi internal-security apparatus kept its access to US-origin equipment. Presidents of both parties also retained discretion to sell arms without the bill's certifications.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Defense exporters and Saudi security agencies

sides.party_line_note: The House vote was overwhelmingly bipartisan: every Democrat present (214) voted yes along with 136 Republicans, while the 71 no votes all came from Republicans.

industries.industry: US defense contractors and arms exporters
industries.note: The bill cuts off new sales, export licenses, and transfers to Saudi intelligence, internal security, and law enforcement agencies unless the President certifies Saudi conduct. But sales for the external defense of Saudi territory are exempt and a national-security waiver is available, so the bulk of the US-Saudi arms trade would have continued; the bill would have hit the industry's internal-security sales most. Its interest in keeping that channel open ran against the bill's protective purpose.

industries.industry: Saudi intelligence, internal security, and law enforcement agencies
industries.note: These agencies would have lost access to US-origin defense articles and services for the duration of the restrictions, unless certified or waived. The US intelligence assessment cited in the bill found these are the organizations linked to the silencing of dissidents abroad.
